messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Farid was 55, a married Middle Eastern man who had spent most of his life working the land, and when he first came to treatment he spoke of his days on the farm with the same practical steadiness that had long organised his life. That steadiness had been disrupted by an assault that he still described only in broken fragments. He could say that there had been men, that they had approached him in a way that felt wrong, that there had been shouting and the sudden shock of being overpowered, but when he tried to tell the full story he would lose the thread and stop mid-sentence, visibly frustrated. He said the memory did not feel like something that had happened to him in the usual sense; it felt as though it belonged to someone else, as if he were trying to recount an event he had only witnessed from a distance. Even now, when he attempted to put the sequence in order, the scene came back in disconnected pieces that did not fit together: a patch of ground, the smell of sweat, a burst of fear, his own heart pounding, and then nothing coherent before the next fragment took over.

In the months that followed, Farid found himself noticing certain moments in ways that startled him. The sensation of his own heart racing could pull him back into the assault before he had time to think. If he bent quickly in the heat and felt his pulse hammering in his chest, or if he became aware of it after lifting produce and working hard in the fields, he would feel a sharp wave of alarm and a sense that danger might be near again. He also became unusually sensitive to the smell of sweat and body odour. At the market, if another man stood close in the queue or passed by after a day’s labour, the smell could catch him unexpectedly and bring back the rough, humiliating feel of the assault in a bodily way he struggled to put into words. He did not describe a clear picture so much as a sudden, distressing return of bodily impressions, leaving him tense and on guard.

Farid became especially troubled by people acting suspiciously. In the village, if a group of men stood talking too quietly, looked in his direction, or lingered outside the farm at an odd hour, he watched them closely and assumed there might be hostility behind their behaviour. What once would have seemed ordinary to him now raised the question of who might be intending harm. He found himself scanning faces and gestures for signs that someone was about to move against him, and this left him feeling unable to relax in places he had always known well. Even around neighbours and workers he knew, he was less at ease, wary of unexpected intentions and quick to interpret ambiguity as possible threat.

Over time, he tried to manage these experiences by throwing himself into work and tasks. He stayed in the fields longer than necessary, found additional jobs around the property, and filled any empty stretch of time with something physical to do. When he was occupied, he felt less room for the memory to intrude. This became particularly marked as dates connected to the assault approached; on anniversaries and other reminders of that period, he made a point of staying busy from dawn until dark. He did not want to sit still and risk being pulled back into the event. In practice, this meant that he worked through meals, took on more than he needed to, and had less time at home than before. His wife noticed that he was present in body but often elsewhere in his mind, and the rhythm of family life narrowed as he organised his days around remaining busy and avoiding the dates that brought the assault sharply into view.

Alongside this, Farid found himself returning again and again to thoughts of revenge. He ruminated about how he might get even with the assailant, imagining confrontations and what he would say if he ever came face to face with the men involved. He did not speak of this with pride; rather, it seemed to occupy him when he was alone, as if his mind would not let go of the insult and fear of that day. He became increasingly preoccupied with the idea that what had happened had left him exposed and disrespected, and the urge to mentally rehearse retaliation was one of the few ways he felt he could push back against what had been done to him.

By the time he sought help, Farid was exhausted by the effort of carrying on in this way. He had continued working, but with a narrowed routine shaped by vigilance, avoidance of anniversaries, and constant attempts to keep himself occupied. He came because the assault still sat with him in fragments that would not settle into a story, because his own racing heart could suddenly make him feel endangered, and because he feared how quickly suspicion and resentment rose in him when something reminded him of that day. What he hoped for was some way to make sense of the memory without feeling that it belonged to someone else, and to reclaim enough calm that he could work and live with his family without always bracing for the next reminder.
